chapters.relation: The editors' introduction surveys Nolan's oeuvre from Doodlebug through Interstellar, arguing that like Socrates's gadfly his films sting viewers out of complacency rather than delivering settled answers. It traces a running theme of self-destruction and self-identity: Buber's I-Thou thesis illuminates Following's Cobb and The Young Man (with a Hegelian master-slave twist), Leonard Shelby in Memento must invent a telos to keep his existence meaningful, Descartes's dream argument stands behind Inception's spinning top, and the Joker voices Hobbes on what 'a little anarchy' does to society. It closes by reading Interstellar as the culmination of these themes, with Cooper's partial love for Murph set against Dr. Mann and Prof. Brand, who are willing to squash their humanity to save the species.

chapters.file: ch04 - Deceit, Desire, and Mimetic Doubling in the Films of Christopher Nolan.md
chapters.relation: Dunn reads Doodlebug's infinite regress of doppelgangers, Following's Cobb manufacturing a double of The Young Man, and The Prestige's Borden-Angier feud as cinematic illustrations of Girard's mimetic theory: we learn what to desire by imitating models, and as model and imitator converge on the same objects they become rivals and doubles. He shows Cobb in Following deliberately certifying The Blonde's desirability to entrap The Young Man (double mediation breeding Cobb's own jealousy), and Fischer's 'desire to be his own man' in Inception being incepted through the mediator of his father. In The Prestige, prestige itself becomes the contested object, a zero-sum metaphysical prize generated by the rivalry that demands escalating sacrifice. Drawing on Augustine's restlessness, Plato's Eros as longing for the Good, and Rousseau's amour-propre, he argues that desire born of ontological lack curdles into rivalry and scapegoating, with Memento's Leonard as the man who deliberately farms fresh scapegoats-in-waiting to keep his actions meaningful.

chapters.file: ch05 - “So You Can Be My ‘John G.’”.md
chapters.relation: Eberl asks whether Leonard Shelby is morally culpable for killing Teddy, since the Leonard who tattoos the false clue and the Leonard who pulls the trigger are sundered by anterograde amnesia. Locke's forensic, memory-based concept of personhood suggests the shooting Leonard is not the same person as the one who set the trap, while Aquinas's analysis of concomitant, consequent, and antecedent ignorance makes Leonard culpable for deliberately willing his own ignorance yet not for the amnesiac moment of the killing itself. Hume's causal criterion of psychological continuity explains why Leonard can still rationally set a goal for his future self by making Teddy his 'John G.' The chapter closes on Aristotle: Leonard's ease in framing an innocent man betrays a corrupted moral character built on habit, and by turning himself into a 'living instrument'—Aristotle's definition of a slave—he has traded his dignity for the telos of an endless revenge quest.

chapters.file: ch06 - White Nights of the Soul.md
chapters.relation: Garcia reads Insomnia as the story of a cop who has lost himself and must choose between two doppelgangers: Walter Finch, the murderer who offers amoral 'partnership' and moral anti-realism ('that ultimate taboo? It doesn't exist outside our minds'), and rookie Ellie Burr, who embodies Dormer's better past as a conscientious policeman. Against Finch's 'moral math' and Dormer's own 'the end justifies the means' rationalizations, the chapter argues that the moral value of actions lies in intentions, motives, and character—Aquinas on what makes a killing an accident, Kant on being worthy of happiness rather than securing it. Dormer's sleeplessness becomes evidence of a conscience still alive, and his struggle figures what Kierkegaard calls purity of heart, willing one thing, with Socrates's refusal to escape in the Crito as the model of integrity. In dying to protect Ellie from losing her way, Dormer regains himself through commitment to another person, the Levinasian point that personhood is fulfilled only in and through other persons.

chapters.file: ch07 - Love, Value, and the Human Destiny in Interstellar.md
chapters.relation: The chapter stages Interstellar's conflict between Cooper's partial love for his own family and Professor Brand's species-level duty as a question about the intrinsic value of humanity. Using Aristotle's account of friends and children as 'other selves' and of happiness as the one end sought for its own sake, it argues that the species survives only as a byproduct of particular, partial loves, so Plan B's bank of 5,000 faceless embryos could not preserve 'us' in any meaningful sense. Kant's unconditional dignity of rational persons supplies Brand's premise that our existence enriches the universe, but the chapter turns Kant against him: Brand's monstrous lie to the Endurance crew treats persons as mere means to an end they do not share, trampling the very dignity it claims to save. It closes by asking what value colonizing Edmunds's planet would destroy—ecosystems, microbial life, and possibly other rational persons whose dignity we would be obliged to respect—should humanity refuse to 'go gentle into that good night.'

chapters.file: ch08 - “They Turned to a Man They Didn’t Fully Understand”.md
chapters.relation: Foy and Dale argue that the Dark Knight trilogy endorses a conservative critique of liberal democracy: Batman taps every citizen's phone, tortures criminals, and kidnaps Lau from Hong Kong because Gotham's institutions cannot cope with a permanent state of crisis. Hume's conservatism—authority resting on habit and order rather than abstract rights and consent—explains Batman's defense of the existing order against Ra's al Ghul's razing of Gotham, while Schmitt's sovereign who declares the 'state of exception' frames Batman as the extra-legal protector who suspends rights during crisis (with Rachel's Caesar warning marking the danger). Against Locke's natural rights and Rawls's inviolability of the person, the Joker and Bane dramatize Strauss's twin fears that liberalism degenerates into nihilistic value-chaos or coercive revolutionary equality, and Burke's natural aristocracy of 'virtual representation' justifies relying on an unchosen elite hero. The trilogy's central puzzle is Batman's illiberal means—taking the blame for Dent's death to preserve the White Knight myth—dirtying his hands so that Gotham's official powers stay clean.

chapters.file: ch09 - The Vale of Top Hats.md
chapters.relation: Decker reads The Prestige's duplication as duplicity: the vale of top hats and the tank-preserved drowned doubles frame an argument that modern stage magic, and Nolan's filmmaking itself, run on the audience's willing self-deception—Robert-Houdin's 'clever man' who pays to be fooled and Nietzsche's artist 'accustomed to lying' meeting man's 'invincible inclination to allow himself to be deceived.' Weber's rationalization and the 'iron cage' supply the chapter's central allegory: Tesla's machine, unlike stage illusion, actually works, embodying a modernity of instrumental cost-benefit calculation in which progress demands ever-costlier sacrifice, making Borden the 'specialist without spirit' and Angier the 'sensualist without heart.' Benjamin's work of art in the age of mechanical reproduction dissolves the question of which Angier is the authentic original, since reproducibility abolishes authenticity and leaves Angier trading the intrinsic value of personhood for transcendence at the price of drowning himself nightly. Benjamin's dictum that every document of culture is also a document of barbarism ties the magicians' art, and Western technological progress from Edison's feuds to the coming World War, to its hidden human cost.

chapters.file: ch10 - Plato, Habermas, and the Demonic Cobb.md
chapters.relation: Murphy treats Following as a provocation keyed to the copy of Plato's Republic glimpsed in The Blonde's apartment: Cobb, who slips unseen into houses and lives and reads people's 'boxes,' is the shepherd with the Ring of Gyges, able to act unjustly without ever facing detection. Against Glaucon's challenge the chapter weighs Socrates's answer that injustice enslaves and disorders the soul—but notes that Nolan shows Cobb victorious, a 'demonic' figure with all of Socrates's abilities and none of his love of justice, who drags Bill and The Blonde into a cave of illusion rather than out of one. Habermas supplies the modern retort: our rationality and sanity depend on the communicative action, truth, and fairness of a shared lifeworld, commitments a sociopathic loner like Cobb cannot renounce without taking refuge in mental illness, though the film never shows Cobb paying that price. Man of Steel's Clark Kent clutching the Republic while letting himself be bullied, and Jonathan Kent's fatal secrecy, become the counterimage of someone who consistently wills justice at personal cost, the closest Nolan comes to showing why justice is worth choosing.

Knight and McKnight analyze how Nolan's early films withhold narrative transparency: Doodlebug's regress of killers, Following's framing device that ends with Cobb vanishing into a crowd, Memento's reverse chronology, and The Prestige's twin frames of top hats and drowned doubles all force viewers to build and revise hypotheses about what happened, when, and who is responsible. Because actions cannot be morally evaluated until we know who performed them and why, the chapter ties narrative comprehension to moral judgment—Leonard's confabulated revenge and inability to recognize his own self-deception, Dormer's ambiguous redemption, and Ellie's unresolved choice over the bullet. The Prestige's doubles raise the identity question the authors gloss with Parfit's teletransporter—perhaps it does not matter which Angier survives—while Cutter's helping Borden kill Caldlow enacts Francis Bacon's 'wild justice' that the law cannot provide. The chapter closes on Nolan as auteur, whose self-conscious framing devices and play of masks make 'Are you watching closely?' at once the film's theme and its admonition to the viewer.

holes.name: Purity of Heart (willing one thing)
holes.what: Kierkegaard's ideal, from 'Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing,' of a will unified in the Good, with harmony and consistency across one's desires, choices, and actions, free of double-mindedness.
holes.why: Chapter 6's subtitle is 'the Struggle for Purity of Heart' and it reads Will Dormer's sleepless moral battle in Insomnia as exactly this Kierkegaardian fight against double-mindedness, with Finch embodying the adaptable double will.

holes.name: Leo Strauss
holes.what: Twentieth-century political philosopher whose critique of liberalism warns that rights-based value pluralism decays into nihilistic relativism, while egalitarian revolutionary movements curdle into tyranny, and who read political order as founded on the friend-enemy distinction.
holes.why: Chapter 8 quotes Strauss's summary of Schmitt at length and structures its whole analysis of the Joker (nihilistic chaos) and Bane (coercive equality) around his two dangers of liberalism.

holes.name: Rationalization and the Iron Cage (disenchantment)
holes.what: Weber's thesis that modern Western culture is dominated by instrumental, cost-benefit rationality which disenchants the world and locks it in an 'iron cage' of efficient, self-imposed institutions, producing 'specialists without spirit, sensualists without heart.'
holes.why: Chapter 9's central allegory reads Tesla's duplication machine and the magicians' economy of sacrifice as an embodiment of Weber's iron cage, but the taxonomy has no concept slug for rationalization, disenchantment, or the iron cage.

holes.name: Fabula and Syuzhet (story vs. discourse)
holes.what: The Russian Formalist narratological distinction between the chronological order of the events narrated (fabula) and the order in which the narrative presents them (syuzhet).
holes.why: Chapter 11's entire analysis of Doodlebug, Following, Memento, and The Prestige rests on this distinction between story chronology and narrative presentation, which taxonomy.json lacks.
